title: Gentler than feared
hookLine: hospice staff often describe dying as a gradual quieting, gentler than many fear

cards: Movies show one version of dying. A gasp. A last speech.
A hand that drops. Monitors screaming. People who work in hospices, the places that care for the dying at the end of life, often describe something else, something quieter and slower.
Not always, and not for everyone. But often enough that they tell families about it ahead of time, so the quiet doesn't frighten them. They call it gentler than many fear.

teach.b: Hospice nurses and doctors describe a gradual winding down in the days or weeks before a death. A person sleeps more and is awake less. They eat less, then drink less.
The body, they explain, is no longer asking for what it once needed, and a family's urge to make someone eat can ease once they know this.

Staff say people near the end often seem to move between sleep and waking, and sometimes speak of people who have already died, or of journeys and travel. They say this is usually not distressing to the person.
Near the very end, they say, breathing often changes: it may slow, pause and start again, or sound rattly as the person can no longer clear their throat. To a family this can sound like suffering.
Hospice staff explain that the person is usually deeply unconscious by then, and they offer care to ease it. And the honest part: not every death is gentle.
Pain, breathlessness and fear do happen, and that's exactly what hospice care exists to treat.
Cicely Saunders, who founded St Christopher's Hospice in London, spoke of total pain: the body's pain, and also the fear, the family worries, the spiritual questions, all tended together.
The British palliative care doctor Kathryn Mannix has written that, with good care, dying is often more peaceful than people fear.
That's not a promise. It's what people who've watched closely report, and knowing it can change what a family is able to do at a bedside.

how: Hospice teams of nurses, doctors, social workers and chaplains care for people at the end of life, at home or in a hospice, and explain to families what to expect as death comes near.

games.q: what hospice staff describe — tap the pairs.
p: more sleep, less food and drink

s: hospice staff describe every death as peaceful
not every death is gentle; pain and fear happen, and care exists to ease them.
eating and drinking less near the end is part of the quieting staff describe
the body is no longer asking for what it once needed.
changed, rattly breathing near the end always means the person is in pain
staff explain the person is usually deeply unconscious by then, and offer care to ease it.

games.q: your grandmother, near the end, has stopped wanting food. your aunt wants to keep pushing her to eat. what do hospice staff explain?
o: the body is winding down and no longer asking for food.
games.why: hospice staff describe eating and drinking less as part of a gradual quieting. knowing that often lets a family stop fighting it.

practice: Let your own breathing set the pace, and notice how it slows a little when nothing is asked of it.
Then let one fact from today come back, the sleeping, the eating less, the breathing, or total pain, and hold the one you'd most want a frightened family to know.

wordCard.voice: Cicely Saunders, who founded St Christopher's Hospice and spoke of total pain, body and fear and family worries tended together. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: a gradual winding down. And for the hard parts, there is care. Day seven hundred ninety-three, done.
